summary: This document defines a YANG data model to configure and manage OSPF. It is based on YANG 1.1 as defined in RFC 7950 and conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture described in RFC 8342.

plainLanguage.summary: OSPF is how routers share maps of the network. This document defines a standard form for configuring it and viewing its state, so that any management tool can drive any OSPF router.

subtitle: A standard YANG schema for configuring OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 routers and reading their state.

tldr.problem: OSPF configuration differs from vendor to vendor, in how a protocol instance is tied to a routing domain and how multiple instances are created, so tools cannot manage routers in one common way.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9129 defines the ietf-ospf YANG module. It augments the core routing model with one OSPF container for configuration and operational state, covering both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3, with optional features, notifications and two RPC operations.
tldr.outcome: Operators and tools get a common interface, over NETCONF, RESTCONF or other protocols, that vendors can extend with their own additions.

today: RFC 9129 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2022. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the OSPF Data Model Is For
sections.content:
YANG (RFC 7950) is a data definition language used to define the contents of a conceptual datastore that allows networked devices to be managed using the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF, RFC 6241), RESTCONF (RFC 8040) and other network management protocols. YANG data models can also be the basis for other interfaces, such as command-line interfaces and programmatic APIs.

This document defines a YANG data model that can be used to configure and manage OSPF. It is an augmentation to the core routing data model defined in RFC 8349, which provides the basis for data models for routing protocols, and it fully conforms to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA, RFC 8342). The interface data model from RFC 8343 is used for referencing interfaces from the routing protocol, and the key chains data model from RFC 8177 is used for OSPF authentication.

Both OSPFv2 (RFC 2328) and OSPFv3 (RFC 5340) are supported. Features described in other OSPF RFCs are supported as well, including demand circuits, Traffic Engineering, multiple address families, graceful restart, the Not-So-Stubby Area option, and OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 as a Provider Edge to Customer Edge protocol. These non-core features are optional in the data model.

The goal is a data model that gives a user interface common to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. Very little information is designated as mandatory, which leaves vendors free to adapt the model to their own implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF is how routers share maps of the network. This document defines a standard form for configuring it and viewing its state, so that any management tool can drive any OSPF router.

sections.title: The Shape of the Model
sections.content:
The OSPF YANG module augments the path /routing/control-plane-protocols/control-plane-protocol defined in the ietf-routing module. The model defines a single instance of OSPF that may be instantiated as an OSPFv2 or an OSPFv3 instance, and multiple instances are instantiated as multiple control-plane protocol instances.

The ospf container holds one OSPF protocol instance, with the router-level configuration and operational state. Below it sit the areas and the topologies containers. The areas container holds a list of areas keyed by area ID, and each area holds its own virtual links, sham links and interfaces. The topologies container holds the OSPF topologies when the multi-topology feature is supported, with a list of topologies keyed by name.

The OSPF operational state is included in the same tree as the OSPF configuration, consistent with the Network Management Datastore Architecture. Consequently only the 'routing' container in the ietf-routing model is augmented; the 'routing-state' container is not.
sections.plainLanguage: The model hangs off the general routing model that every routing protocol uses. Under one OSPF entry sit the areas, and under each area sit the interfaces.

sections.title: OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 in One Model
sections.content:
The data model defined here supports both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3. The 'version' field indicates which OSPF version is in use and is mandatory. Based on the configured version, the data model varies to accommodate the differences between the two.

The effect is visible in the Link State Database, where the decoded link state advertisements are grouped by version: the OSPFv2 form has a header, a body with router, network, summary, external and opaque sections, while the OSPFv3 form has a header, a body with router, network, inter-area prefix, inter-area router, as-external, NSSA, link, intra-area prefix and router-information sections.
sections.plainLanguage: The same model covers both versions of OSPF. A field says which version is running, and the parts of the model that differ are then shown for that version.

sections.title: Optional Features
sections.content:
Optional features go beyond the basic OSPF configuration, and it is the responsibility of each vendor to decide whether to support a given feature on a particular device. The model defines a long list of them.

They include multi-topology routing, multi-area adjacencies, an explicit per-instance router ID, demand circuits, disabling of the Database Description packet MTU mismatch check, link-local signaling, prefix advertisement suppression, TTL security checking, Non-Stop Routing, graceful restart, interface cost calculation from a reference bandwidth, configuration of the maximum number of equal-cost paths, configuration of the maximum number of link state advertisements accepted, the Traffic Engineering router ID, LDP IGP synchronization, the OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 authentication trailers, IPsec for OSPFv3 authentication, IP Fast Reroute, node flags, node tags, loop-free alternates, remote loop-free alternates, stub router advertisements, OSPF as a PE-CE protocol, the IETF shortest path first delay algorithm, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection for neighbour reachability, and hybrid broadcast and point-to-multipoint interfaces.

It is expected that vendors will support further features through vendor-specific augmentations.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of OSPF is described as always present. The extra features, from multi-topology to fast reroute, are marked optional, and each vendor decides which to support on which device.

sections.title: Router, Area and Interface Containers
sections.content:
The ospf container is the top-level container in the model. It represents an OSPF protocol instance and holds the router-level configuration and operational state. The operational state includes instance statistics, IETF SPF delay statistics, the AS-Scope Link State Database, the local RIB, the SPF log and the LSA log.

The router-level configuration covers the address family, whether the instance is enabled, an optional explicit router ID, the administrative preference for the routes the instance installs, Non-Stop Routing and graceful restart settings, automatic cost calculation with a reference bandwidth, SPF control including the maximum number of paths and the SPF delay parameters, a database control setting for the maximum number of link state advertisements, stub router advertisement triggers, MPLS settings including the Traffic Engineering router ID and LDP IGP synchronization, fast reroute settings and node tags.

The area container holds the area configuration and the list of interface containers for the OSPF interfaces in that area, and the area operational state includes area statistics and the area Link State Database. An area holds its area ID, an optional area type, a summary flag, a default cost, a list of ranges with their prefix, advertise flag and cost, optional topologies, virtual links and sham links.

The interface container holds the interface configuration and operational state, and the interface operational state includes the interface statistics, the list of neighbours and the link-local Link State Database. The configuration covers the interface reference, interface type, passive and demand-circuit flags, priority, multi-area adjacencies, static neighbours, node flags, BFD settings, fast reroute settings, the hello, dead, retransmit and transmit timers, link-local signaling, TTL security, the enabled flag, authentication, the link cost, MTU ignore and prefix suppression. The operational state adds the interface state, the timers, the designated and backup router identifiers and addresses, statistics, neighbours and the link-scoped database.
sections.plainLanguage: The model follows the shape of OSPF itself: one instance, the areas inside it, and the interfaces inside each area. Configuration and the current state sit side by side, so a client can read and change the same tree.

sections.title: Notifications and RPC Operations
sections.content:
The data model defines a list of notifications that inform YANG clients of important events detected during protocol operation. The defined notifications cover the common set of traps from the OSPFv2 MIB (RFC 4750) and the OSPFv3 MIB (RFC 5643).

They are if-state-change and if-config-error for the interfaces, nbr-state-change and nbr-restart-helper-status-change for the neighbours, if-rx-bad-packet for a bad packet received, lsdb-approaching-overflow and lsdb-overflow for the Link State Database, nssa-translator-status-change for the NSSA translator, and restart-status-change for a graceful restart. Each notification carries the routing protocol name and the address family, and then the details that apply: the interface, virtual link or sham link involved, the state, the packet source and type, the neighbour router ID and address, and the reason or exit reason where one applies.

The module defines two RPC operations. clear-database resets the contents of a particular OSPF Link State Database, forces neighbour adjacencies to the 'DOWN' state, and reoriginates self-originated link state advertisements. clear-neighbor resets a particular OSPF neighbour or group of neighbours associated with an OSPF interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The model can tell a client when something happens, such as a neighbour changing state or the database filling up. It also offers two commands that a client can run: one to clear a database and one to reset a neighbour.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module defines a schema for data designed to be accessed through network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, whose mandatory-to-implement secure transport is Secure Shell, and the lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS with TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (RFC 8341) provides the means to restrict access for particular users to a preconfigured subset of the available operations and content.

Many data nodes are writable, creatable or deletable, and may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Write operations to them without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. For OSPF, the ability to modify the configuration allows the entire OSPF domain to be compromised, including peering with unauthorized routers to misroute traffic or to mount a denial-of-service attack; adding OSPF on an unprotected interface could allow an adjacency to form with an unauthorized and malicious neighbour, and once an adjacency is formed traffic could be hijacked. A simpler example is a denial-of-service attack mounted by making the cost of an interface asymmetric, so that a hard routing loop ensues.

Some readable data nodes may also be sensitive. Exposure of the Link State Database exposes the detailed topology of the network, and in the case of an area database the complete IP network topology, and the Traffic Engineering topology if deployed, can be reconstructed. Network operators may consider their topologies to be sensitive confidential data.

For authentication, configuration is supported through key chains or by directly specifying a key and an algorithm, and the second option inherits the security considerations of the key chains specification, including the local storage and handling of keys. It is RECOMMENDED that implementations migrate to key chains, because that gives seamless support of key and algorithm rollover, a hexadecimal key specification that affords more key entropy, and encryption of keys with the AES Key Wrap with Padding algorithm.

Access to the clear-neighbor and clear-database operations should also be controlled, because if access is compromised, temporary network outages can be used to mount denial-of-service attacks. The actual authentication key data is sensitive and needs to be kept secret, because compromise of the key data would allow an attacker to forge OSPF traffic that would be accepted as authentic, potentially compromising the entire OSPF domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing OSPF configuration is powerful enough to take over a whole network, and the database reveals the shape of the network. Access to both needs to be restricted, and the authentication keys need to be kept secret.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The document registers a URI in the IETF XML Registry: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-ospf, with the IESG as registrant contact and the note that the requested URI is an XML namespace.

It also registers a YANG module in the YANG Module Names registry, with the name ietf-ospf, the same namespace, the prefix ospf and RFC 9129 as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The XML namespace list and the list of YANG module names each get one new entry for this document.

items.label: Interface configuration error
items.desc: A bad packet or a configuration error was seen, with the packet source and type.

items.label: Neighbour state change
items.desc: A neighbour changed state, with its router ID and address.

items.label: Restart helper status
items.desc: The status of the restart helper for a neighbour changed.

items.label: Bad packet received
items.desc: A malformed packet was received on an interface.

items.label: Database approaching overflow
items.desc: The Link State Database is close to its configured limit.

items.label: Database overflow
items.desc: The Link State Database reached its configured limit.

items.label: NSSA translator status
items.desc: The NSSA translator status changed for an area.

items.label: Restart status
items.desc: The graceful restart status changed, with the reason.
